label: ns_max
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \textsf{$L^2$ endpoint and $L^p$ maximal inequalities

title: Remark
body_md:
\rm
(i) The constant $C_{d, K}$ in  the endpoint estimate
\eqref{ns_l2} is uniform in $f\in L^2(\gamma)$ and
in the   covariance matrix, subject to the Hermite-rank
condition and row-sum bound \eqref{ns_rows}.
The exponent $p=2$ is critical for the usual dyadic maximal
argument.  A block estimate of order $\sqrt{|I|}$ in $L^p$
produces the factors $2^{-j(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p})}$ at level
$j$.  These form a summable geometric series for $p>2$;
at $p=2$ the decay disappears, so summation over the dyadic
levels produces a logarithmic loss.\footnote{The geometric
series is evaluated in \eqref{lp_geometric} and used in
\eqref{lp_max_proof}.  At $p=2$, its finite counterpart has
$L+1$ terms, where $L$ is of order $\log n$.}
Indeed, from the orthogonality relation \eqref{OL_pq},
we can deduce that
$\|\sum_{i\in I}f(Z_i)\|^2_2
 \le\|f\|_2^2\sum_{i,j\in I}|\mathbb{E}[Z_iZ_j]|^d
 \le K|I|\,\|f\|_2^2$,
and direct dyadic summation gives only
$C\sqrt{Kn}\log(2n)\|f\|_2$ for the maximal $L^2$ norm.
The main estimate \eqref{ns_l2} removes this logarithmic loss
under the sole finite-variance assumption.
It is the key input used for
the BMD principles in Section~\ref{bm_intro}.

\smallskip

(ii) For independent Gaussian coordinates, \eqref{ns_l2} follows
from Doob's inequality.  In the dependent setting, the partial
sums of $f(Z_k)$ are generally not martingales, so neither
Doob's inequality nor the Burkholder--Davis--Gundy inequalities
\cite{BDG72} apply directly; see
\cite[Chapters~II and~IV]{RY99} for standard treatments.
The right-hand side of \eqref{ns_l2} is $n\|f\|_2^2$, not the terminal variance.
For $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, the choice $Z_1=G$, $Z_2=-G$, and
$f(x)=x$ satisfies \eqref{ns_rows} with $d=1$, $K=2$, but the
terminal sum is zero and the maximal partial sum is $|G|$.
Gaussian entropy and concentration inequalities
  give the bound when $f(x)=ax$ and
$d=1$; see, e.g.,  \cite[Chapters~1--2]{AT07}.
For nonlinear $f$, however, the partial-sum process need not
be Gaussian, and square integrability alone does not supply
sub-Gaussian increment control.  For a fixed finite Hermite
expansion, Nelson's hypercontractivity, followed
by a higher-moment maximal argument, gives a bound with a
constant depending on the Hermite cutoff; see
\cite[Section~2.8]{NP12}.  The endpoint \eqref{ns_l2} controls
the full $L^2(\gamma)$ class of the prescribed  Hermite rank 
uniformly in that cutoff.
 


\smallskip

(iii) The resulting $\sqrt n$ scale agrees with that for independent
sums and square-integrable martingales, and is optimal: for
independent standard Gaussian coordinates and $f=h_d$, the
terminal sum already has $L^2$ norm $\sqrt n$.

label: bm_thm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{bm_thm}
Assume that $\varphi\in L^2(\gamma)$ has Hermite rank $d\ge1$ as in
\eqref{d_phi} and $\rho_G\in\ell^d(\mathbb{Z})$.  Then the
finite-dimensional distributions of $V_n$ converge to those of
$\sigma_G\mathcal{W}$, where
\begin{align}\label{d_var}
 \sigma_G^2
 =\sum_{q=d}^{\infty}q!c_q^2
   \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\rho_G(k)^q
 \in[0,\infty).
\end{align}
head: environment
name: \textsf{Breuer--Major theorem

label: disc_thm
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{disc_thm}
Let $\mathbf G$ be a centered stationary Gaussian sequence with
covariance function $\rho_G$, and let $V_n$ be as in \eqref{d_V},
with $\varphi\in L^2(\gamma)$ having Hermite rank $d\ge1$ as in
\eqref{d_phi}.  Assume that $\rho_G(0)=1$ and
\begin{align}\label{d_bm}
 \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}|\rho_G(k)|^d<\infty.
\end{align}
Then, as $n\to+\infty$,   $V_n\Longrightarrow\sigma_G\mathcal{W}$ in  $\mathbf D([0,1])$,
where $\sigma_G^2$ is given by \eqref{d_var}.  The family $(V_n)$ is
$C$-tight.  Moreover, with $\widehat{V_n}$ as in \eqref{hat_V},
 $\widehat{V_n}\Longrightarrow\sigma_G\mathcal{W}$
 in $\mathbf C([0,1])$.
head: environment
name: \textsf{Finite-variance discrete BMD principle

label: cont_thm
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cont_thm}
Let $\mathbf B$ be a jointly measurable, centered Gaussian process with
covariance structure \eqref{c_cov} and \eqref{c_bm}. 
Let $\varphi\in L^2(\gamma)$ have Hermite rank $d\ge1$ as in
\eqref{d_phi}.
Then, as $T\to\infty$,
$ V_T\Longrightarrow\sigma_{\varphi,B}\mathcal{W}$
in $\mathbf C([0,1]),$
where $\sigma_{\varphi,B}^2$ is given by \eqref{c_var}.
head: environment
name: \textsf{Finite-variance continuous-time BMD principle

label: path_cor
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{path_cor}
If $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$ and $f-g$ has Hermite rank at least $d$,
then, under \eqref{ns_rows},
\begin{align}\label{path_l2}
 \mathbb{E} \big[   \|\mathcal S_n^f-\mathcal S_n^g\|_\infty^2 \big]
 \le C_{d,K}\|f-g\|_2^2.
\end{align}
The constant is uniform over all $n$ and all covariance matrices
satisfying \eqref{ns_rows}.  In particular, for
$\varphi_M=\sum_{q=d}^M c_qH_q$,
\begin{align}\label{path_tail}
 \sup_n\mathbb{E}  \big[   \|\mathcal S_n^\varphi
                  -\mathcal S_n^{\varphi_M}\|_\infty^2 \big]
 \le C_{d,K}\sum_{q>M}q!c_q^2\xrightarrow{M\to+\infty}0.
\end{align}

\noindent
The same estimates hold for the polygonal paths
$\widehat{\mathcal S}_n^f$, obtained by linear interpolation of
$\mathcal S_n^f$ at $0, 1/n, 2/n,\ldots,1$.
head: environment
name: \textsf{Uniform approximation in path norm

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying   \eqref{ns_l2} to $f-g$  yields  \eqref{path_l2} immediately.  
The orthogonality relation \eqref{OL_pq}
then implies  \eqref{path_tail}.
On each grid interval,
the difference of the polygonal paths is affine, so its
absolute maximum is attained at an endpoint.  Thus its
supremum equals that of the difference of the step paths.
Hence, the proof is completed.

label: rearr_lem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{rearr_lem}
For each fixed integer  $q\ge0$, there is a constant $C_q$ such that the
following
statements hold.

\smallskip
\textup{(i)} If $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ is measurable and
$p=\gamma(A)\in (0, \frac{1}{2}]$, then
\begin{align}\label{set_rearr}
  \int_A h_q(x)^2\,\gamma(dx)
  \le C_qp\bigl(1+\log(1/p)\bigr)^q.
\end{align}

\textup{(ii)} Suppose  $U$ is a nonnegative random variable
with  $U\le M$ and $\mathbb{E}[U]\le C_0$
for some deterministic constants $C_0$ and $M\geq 2$.
Then,
\begin{align}\label{wt_rearr}
  \mathbb{E}[U|h_q(\mathcal Z)|]
  \le C_{q,C_0}(1+\log M)^{\frac{q}{2}},
\end{align}
where $\mathcal Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

label: diag_lem
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{diag_lem}
Let $\mathcal{I}$ be a countable index set,
and let
 $(Z_j)_{j\in\mathcal I}$ be a   centered Gaussian
family with standard normal marginals.
Define
$r(i,j)=\mathbb{E}[Z_iZ_j]$ for $i,j\in\mathcal{I}$.
 Suppose that there is some $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{3})$ such that
\begin{align}\label{small_c1}
 \sup_{i\ne j}|r(i,j)|\le\varepsilon ,
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}\label{small_c2}
   K_d:=\sup_{i\in\mathcal I}
       \sum_{j\in\mathcal I}|r(i,j)|^d<\infty.
\end{align}
Given $A\subset\mathcal I$  with cardinality
$|A|  \leq m$,
the following statements hold, with
a constant $C$ depending only on $d$, $\varepsilon$, and $K_d$,
where
a prime on a multiple sum means that all
displayed indices are pairwise distinct.

\smallskip
\textup{(i)} If $f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4\in L^2(\gamma)$ have Hermite rank at
least
$d$, then
\begin{align}\label{diag4}
  \sum_{t_1,\ldots,t_4\in A}'
  \left|\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^4f_i(Z_{t_i})\right]\right|
  \le Cm^2\prod_{i=1}^4\|f_i\|_2.
\end{align}

\textup{(ii)} If $f_0,f_1,f_2\in L^2(\gamma)$ all have Hermite rank at least
$d$, then
\begin{align}\label{diag3}
 \sum_{x,y,z\in A}'
 |\mathbb{E}[f_0(Z_x)f_1(Z_y)f_2(Z_z)]|
 \le Cm^{\frac{3}{2}}\prod_{i=0}^2\|f_i\|_2.
\end{align}

\textup{(iii)}    Let $1\le s<d$ and $B=bh_s$ for some $b\in\mathbb{R}$,
where $h_s$ is given as in \eqref{def_hq}.
Let $f_1,f_2\in L^2(\gamma)$ have
Hermite rank at least $d$.  Then
\begin{align}\label{diag_mix}
 \sum_{x,y,z\in A}'
 |\mathbb{E}[B(Z_x)f_1(Z_y)f_2(Z_z)]|
 \le C |b|    m^{2-\frac{s}{2d}}\|f_1\|_2\|f_2\|_2.
\end{align}
head: environment
name: \textsf{Separated diagram bounds

title: Proof
body_md:
For parts~\textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)}, we can apply
\cite[Lemma~1]{BS13a} with scalar coordinates, common rank threshold $d$,
and all $p$ functions subject to that threshold, where $p=4$ and $p=3$,
respectively.  That result applies to nonstationary Gaussian arrays.  In
its notation, $\nu=1$, $\alpha=p$, and
\begin{align*}
 Q_A:=\max_{t\in A}\sum_{s\in A\setminus\{t\}}|r(t,s)|^d\le K_d
\end{align*}
with $K_d$ as in \eqref{small_c2}.
Its small-correlation hypothesis is $\varepsilon<\frac{1}{p-1}$, which is
satisfied by
$\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{3})$.
As a consequence, we have
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t_1,\ldots,t_p\in A}'
 \left|\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^pf_i(Z_{t_i})\right|
 \le C|A|^{\frac{p}{2}}Q_A^{\frac{p}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^p\|f_i\|_2.
\end{align*}
This gives \eqref{diag4} and \eqref{diag3}.

\medskip

We next prove part~\textup{(iii)}.  We first assume that $f_1$ and
$f_2$ have finite Hermite expansions:
\begin{align*}
 f_1=\sum_{q\ge d}u_qh_q,\quad
 f_2=\sum_{\ell\ge d}v_\ell h_\ell .
\end{align*}

\noindent
Recall that
\begin{align*}
 \|B\|_2=|b|,\quad
 \|f_1\|_2^2=\sum_{q\ge d}u_q^2,
 \quad{\rm and}\quad
 \|f_2\|_2^2=\sum_{\ell\ge d}v_\ell^2.
\end{align*}

Let us first represent the Gaussian family as
$
 Z_j= \mathcal{X} (e_j)
 $,
 where $\mathcal{X} $ is an isonormal Gaussian process over a real separable Hilbert
 space
$\mathfrak H$ and
the 
$\{e_j\}$ are unit vectors such that
 $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle_{\mathfrak H}=r(i,j)$;
see \cite[Proposition 7.2.3]{NP12}.  Since
$
 h_q(Z_j)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{q!}}I_q(e_j^{\otimes q}),
$
we deduce from the product formula \cite[Theorem 2.7.10]{NP12} that

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 h_q(Z_y)h_\ell(Z_z)
 &=
 \frac{1}{\sqrt{q!\ell!}}
 \sum_{c=0}^{q\wedge\ell}
 c!\binom qc\binom\ell c
 r(y,z)^c
 I_{q+\ell-2c}\big( e_y^{\otimes(q-c)}  \widetilde{\otimes}
 e_z^{\otimes(\ell-c)}  \big),
\end{align*}

\noindent
where  $e_y^{\otimes(q-c)}  \widetilde{\otimes}  e_z^{\otimes(\ell-c)} $
is the symmetrization of $e_y^{\otimes(q-c)}  \otimes
e_z^{\otimes(\ell-c)}$.
Then, we deduce from  the orthogonality relation
\cite[Proposition 2.7.5]{NP12} that
 only the value of $c$
satisfying
$q+\ell-2c=s$
can contribute to $\mathbb{E}[ h_s(Z_x) h_q(Z_y)h_\ell(Z_z) ]$.
Put
 $\alpha=q-c$ and $\beta=\ell-c.$
Then,
$q+\ell-2c=s$ is equivalent to
\begin{align}\label{deg_rel}
 \alpha+\beta=s,\quad
 q=\alpha+c,\quad
 \ell=\beta+c.
\end{align}
In particular, since $q,\ell\ge d$,
we have
\begin{align}\label{c_low}
 c\ge d-\min(\alpha,\beta).
 \end{align}
 Since
$ \langle
 e_y^{\otimes\alpha}\widetilde{\otimes}
 e_z^{\otimes\beta},
 e_x^{\otimes s}
  \rangle_{\mathfrak H^{\otimes s}}
 = \langle
 e_y^{\otimes\alpha} \otimes
 e_z^{\otimes\beta},
 e_x^{\otimes s}
  \rangle_{\mathfrak H^{\otimes s}}
 =
 r(x,y)^\alpha r(x,z)^\beta$ for $\alpha + \beta =s$,
 we have
\begin{align}\label{3diag_exact}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb{E}[h_s(Z_x)h_{\alpha+c}(Z_y)h_{\beta+c}(Z_z)]
& = \frac{c! \binom{\alpha+c}{c} \binom{\beta+c}{c} s!}{ \sqrt{s! (\alpha+c)!
(\beta+c)! }}
 r(x,y)^\alpha r(x,z)^\beta r(y,z)^c
\\
&= \frac{\sqrt{s!(\alpha+c)!(\beta+c)!}}{\alpha!\beta!c!}\,
 r(x,y)^\alpha r(x,z)^\beta r(y,z)^c.
\end{aligned}
\end{align}
Again by  $\alpha+\beta=s$, the factorial coefficient in
\eqref{3diag_exact} satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\sqrt{s!(\alpha+c)!(\beta+c)!}}{\alpha!\beta!c!}
 =  \frac{\sqrt{s!}}{\alpha!\beta!}
 \left(    \frac{(\alpha+c)!}{c!}   \frac{(\beta+c)!}{c!}
 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}
 \leq C_s(1+c)^{\frac{s}{2}}.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\begin{align}\label{wick3}
 \big|   \mathbb{E}[h_s(Z_x)h_{\alpha+c}(Z_y)h_{\beta+c}(Z_z)]  \big|
\leq   C_s(1+c)^{s/2}
 |r(x,y)|^\alpha
 |r(x,z)|^\beta
 |r(y,z)|^c.
\end{align}

We next sum the correlation factors over the distinct indices.
Since $\alpha+\beta=s$, at least one of $\alpha,\beta$ is at least $s/2$.
Without loss of generality, let us assume
$
 \beta\geq  s/2,
$
while the case $\alpha\geq  s/2$ can be dealt with in the same way.
With $\beta\geq s/2$,
we have
 $\beta\ge\alpha$, and thus
$c\ge d-\alpha$ by \eqref{c_low}.
 For fixed distinct $x,z$,
 it follows from
\eqref{small_c1}
that

\noindent
\begin{align*}
\sum_{y\in A\setminus\{x,z\}}
 |r(x,y)|^\alpha |r(y,z)|^c
\leq
 \varepsilon^{\alpha+c-d}
 \sum_{y\in A\setminus\{x,z\}}
 |r(x,y)|^\alpha |r(y,z)|^{d-\alpha}.
\end{align*}
If $1\le\alpha<d$, we can deduce from H\"older's inequality
that

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_y
 |r(x,y)|^\alpha |r(y,z)|^{d-\alpha}
\leq
 \left(\sum_y|r(x,y)|^d\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{d}}
 \left(\sum_y|r(y,z)|^d\right)^{\frac{d-\alpha}{d}}\le K_d,
\end{align*}
with $K_d$ as in \eqref{small_c2}.
The same bound is also immediate for $\alpha=0$.  Thus,
\begin{align}\label{conv_bd}
 \sup_{x\ne z}
 \sum_{y\in A\setminus\{x,z\}}
 |r(x,y)|^\alpha |r(y,z)|^c
 \le K_d\varepsilon^{\alpha+c-d}.
\end{align}

We now sum the remaining factor $|r(x,z)|^\beta$.  By H\"older's inequality,
we have
\begin{align}
 \sum_{x,z\in A}
 |r(x,z)|^\beta \mathbf{1}_{\{x\ne z\}}
& \le
 |A|^{2-2\frac{\beta}{d}}
 \Bigg(
   \sum_{x,z\in A }
   |r(x,z)|^d\mathbf{1}_{\{x\ne z\}}
 \Bigg)^{\frac{\beta}{d}} \notag \\
& \le
 |A|^{2-2\frac{\beta}{d}}(|A|K_d)^{\frac{\beta}{d}}  \notag  \\
& \leq
 C m^{2-\frac{\beta}{d}} \leq   C m^{2-\frac{s}{2d}}.
 \label{edge_sum}
\end{align}
Here, $\beta\le s<d$ by \eqref{deg_rel},
so that the factor $K_d^{\beta/d}$, bounded by $\max\{1, K_d\}$,
 can be absorbed into
the constant $C$. The last inequality in \eqref{edge_sum}
is due to   $\beta\ge s/2$.

Combining \eqref{conv_bd} and \eqref{edge_sum}, and interchanging
$y,z$ when $\alpha>\beta$, yields
\begin{align}\label{fixed_diagram_sum}
 &\sum_{x,y,z\in A}'
 |r(x,y)|^\alpha
 |r(x,z)|^\beta
 |r(y,z)|^c
 \leq
 C\varepsilon^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}+c-d}
 m^{2-\frac{s}{2d}}.
\end{align}

\smallskip

We finally sum over the Hermite orders.
In view of \eqref{wick3} and \eqref{fixed_diagram_sum},
each fixed pair
$(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha+\beta=s$ contributes to the left side of
\eqref{diag_mix},
and its contribution is bounded by

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 &C|b|m^{2-\frac{s}{2d}}
 \sum_{c\ge d-\min(\alpha,\beta)}
 |u_{\alpha+c}v_{\beta+c}|
 (1+c)^{\frac{s}{2}}\varepsilon^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}+c-d}.
\end{align*}

\noindent
Since $\varepsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{3})$, we have

\noindent
\begin{align*}
\sup_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\ge0\\ \alpha+\beta=s}} \sup_{c\ge d- \min\{\alpha,\beta\}}
 (1+c)^{\frac{s}{2}}\varepsilon^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}+c-d}
 <\infty.
\end{align*}
Therefore, we can apply the above uniform bound
and  Cauchy--Schwarz to get
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{c\ge d-\min\{\alpha,\beta\}}
 |u_{\alpha+c}v_{\beta+c}|
 (1+c)^{\frac{s}{2}}\varepsilon^{\min\{\alpha,\beta\}+c-d}
&\leq
 C_{d,s,\varepsilon}
 \bigg(\sum_{q\ge d}u_q^2\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}
 \bigg(\sum_{\ell\ge d}v_\ell^2\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
&=
 C_{d,s,\varepsilon}\|f_1\|_2\|f_2\|_2.
\end{align*}
There are only finitely many pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ with
$\alpha+\beta=s$.
As a result, we get

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{diag_mix_finite}
 \sum_{x,y,z\in A}'
 |\mathbb{E}[B(Z_x)f_1(Z_y)f_2(Z_z)]|
 \le
 C|b|m^{2- \frac{s}{2d}}
 \|f_1\|_2\|f_2\|_2,
\end{align}
when $f_1, f_2$ have finite Hermite expansions, or equivalently,
when they are polynomials.
Note that the constant $C$ in \eqref{diag_mix_finite}
does not depend on the degrees of the polynomials $f_1, f_2$.

It remains to remove the finite-expansion assumption.  Let
$f_{1,N} = \sum_{q=d}^N u_q h_q$
and $f_{2,N} = \sum_{\ell=d}^N v_\ell h_\ell$.
 Then,
 $f_{i,N} \to f_i$
in  $L^2(\gamma)$
and
$ \|f_{i,N}\|_2\le\|f_i\|_2$ for $i=1,2$.

For distinct $x,y,z$, let $\Sigma$ be the covariance matrix of
$(Z_x,Z_y,Z_z)$.   By \eqref{small_c1} and Gershgorin's circle theorem
(see, e.g., \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Var04}),
the spectrum of the covariance matrix $\Sigma$
is contained in $ [1-2\varepsilon,1+2\varepsilon]\subset(0,2)$.
In particular, $\Sigma$ is positive definite, so the law of
$(Z_x,Z_y,Z_z)$ is nondegenerate and admits a density $L$ with
respect to $\gamma^{\otimes3}$.  Moreover, the operator norm $\|\Sigma\|<2$ implies that
$2\Sigma^{-1}-I$ is positive definite, and hence
$L\in L^2(\gamma^{\otimes3})$.
Consequently,

\noindent
\begin{align*}
\Big\vert  \mathbb{E}\big[
& B(Z_x)(f_{1,N}-f_1)(Z_y)f_{2,N}(Z_z)  \big] \Big\vert  \\
 &= \left\vert  \int_{\mathbb{R}^3 } B(w_1)(f_{1,N}-f_1)(w_2)f_{2,N}(w_3) L(w_1,
 w_2, w_3) \gamma^{\otimes 3}(dw_1, dw_2, dw_3) \right\vert\\
 & \le
  \| L\|_2  |b|
 \|f_{1,N}-f_1\|_2
 \|f_{2,N}\|_2
 \xrightarrow{N\to+\infty}0,
\end{align*}
and the analogous estimate holds for the second factor.  Thus,
for every distinct triple $(x,y,z)$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}[B(Z_x)f_{1,N}(Z_y)f_{2,N}(Z_z)]
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb{E}[B(Z_x)f_1(Z_y)f_2(Z_z)].
\end{align*}
Since the primed sum over $A$ is finite, we may pass to the limit
in \eqref{diag_mix_finite}.  This proves \eqref{diag_mix} and
hence  completes the proof of Lemma  \ref{diag_lem}.
\qedhere
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\rm
Parts~\textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} of Lemma~\ref{diag_lem}
are direct consequences of
\cite[Lemma~1]{BS13a}, since all factors have Hermite rank at least
$d$.  Part~\textup{(iii)} requires a refinement.
Indeed, applying \cite[Lemma~1]{BS13a} with $p=3$ and only
$f_1,f_2$ subject to the Hermite-rank-$d$ condition
(that is, with $\alpha=2$ in the notation of \cite{BS13a})
would yield only an $O(m^2)$ bound.  Here we exploit the
additional fact that the remaining factor $B=bh_s$ belongs to the
single chaos of order $s<d$.  In the three-row diagram expansion the
edge multiplicities satisfy $\alpha+\beta=s$, so one of $\alpha,\beta$ is at
least $s/2$.  Retaining the corresponding correlation power and
using
the $d$th-power covariance row bound yields the additional factor
$m^{-\frac{s}{2d}}$, and hence the sharper bound
$m^{2-\frac{s}{2d}}$.

title: Lemma
head: environment
name: \textsf{Adjacent-block maximal lemma

label: rem_mor
title: Remark
body_md:
\rm
\label{rem_mor}
It is useful to compare  Lemma \ref{max_lem}
with the classical
moment-to-maximum inequality of M\'oricz
\cite[Theorem~1]{Mor76}.  In a simplified form, M\'oricz's result
starts from a one-block moment estimate
$
 \mathbb{E}|S_I|^p\le C|I|^\beta
 $
 with 
 $\beta>1$,
and yields a maximal estimate of the same power order.
In the present setting, the natural one-block estimate is only
$
 \mathbb{E}[S_I^2]\le C|I|.
$
Thus the one-block second moment lies at the borderline $\beta=1$,
and the elementary dyadic argument based on this estimate gives
$\mathbb{E}\big[ \max_{m\le N}|S_{(0,m]}|^2 \big] \leq C N(\log(2N))^2.$
Uniform finite-variance approximation therefore requires a
sharper maximal bound.


 

The additional information available here has a different form.
For adjacent disjoint blocks $I,J$, we prove the bound \eqref{abs_adj},
in which the strict power gain is  sufficient
to recover the diffusive maximal bound \eqref{abs_max}
through a dyadic argument.
In this sense,  Lemma \ref{max_lem} is complementary to M\'oricz's principle:
M\'oricz exploits a superlinear moment bound for a single block,
whereas here the single-block second moment remains linear and the
strict gain appears only after coupling two adjacent blocks.

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is divided into three steps.  Throughout, $(\ell,r]$
denotes the integer interval $(\ell,r]\cap\mathbb N$.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\bf Step 1: Reduction to a two-sided cut maximal function.}
Choose the smallest dyadic integer $M=2^L$ such that $M\ge N$,
so that $N\le M<2N$, and set
$X_k=0$ for $N<k\le M$.  This allows us to work on a complete
dyadic tree down to singleton intervals, while changing the relevant
scales only by an absolute constant.
For an integer interval $D=(\ell,r]\subset(0,M]$, define
\begin{align}\label{cut_def}
 R(D)
 :=
 \max_{\ell\le m\le r}
 \min\big\{
 |S_{(\ell,m]}|,
 |S_{(m,r]}|
 \big\}.
\end{align}
Thus $R(D)$ measures, over all cuts of $D$, the largest possible
value of the smaller of the two partial sums created by the cut.

Define  $P_m=\sum_{k=1}^mX_k$.
Then, we have
$S_{(0,m]}=P_m$ and
$S_{(m,M]}=P_N-P_m.$
Therefore,
$\min\{|P_m|,|P_N-P_m|\}\le R((0,M])$.
Moreover,
\begin{align}\label{prefix_bd}
 |P_m|
 \le
 |P_N|
 +
 \min\{|P_m|,|P_N-P_m|\}
 \le
 |P_N|+R((0,M]).
\end{align}

\noindent
Hence,  due to Assumption \eqref{abs_var}, it remains to prove
$
 \|R((0,M])\|_2 \leq C\sqrt N.
$

\smallskip
\noindent
{\bf Step 2: Dyadic recursion for the cut maximal function.}
Let $D=(\ell,r]$ be a dyadic interval,
 $a=\frac{\ell+r}{2}$,
and write $D^-=(\ell,a]$ and $D^+=(a,r]$.
Set $z_D= \min\{|S_{D^-}|,|S_{D^+}|\}.$
We claim that
\begin{align}\label{dy_rec}
 R(D)
 \le
 z_D+\max\{R(D^-),R(D^+)\}.
\end{align}

To prove this, first note the elementary inequality\footnote{To
verify \eqref{min_ineq}, if $|a|\le |b|$, then it is immediate.
  If $|b|<|a|$, then
$
 \min\{|a|,|b+c|\}-|b|
 =\min\{|a|-|b|,\ |b+c|-|b|\}
 \le\min\{|a+b|,\ |c|\},
$
which implies \eqref{min_ineq}.}
\begin{align}\label{min_ineq}
 \min\{|a|,|b+c|\}
 \le
 \min\{|a|,|b|\}
 +
 \min\{|a+b|,|c|\}.
\end{align}

Consider  $m\in D^-$.  Then,
we apply   \eqref{min_ineq}
with $a_1:=S_{(\ell,m]}$, $b_1:=S_{(m,a]}$, and
$c_1:=S_{D^+}$
to get

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \min\big\{  |S_{(\ell,m]}|,   |S_{(m,r]}|  \big\}
 =  \min\big\{  |a_1 |,   |b_1 + c_1 |  \big\}
 &\leq
 \min\{|a_1|,|b_1|\} +  \min\{|a_1+b_1|,|c_1|\} \\
 & \leq R(D^-)+z_D.
\end{align*}

\noindent
For $m\in D^+$, the same argument  yields
$\min\big\{ |S_{(\ell,m]}|,   |S_{(m,r]}| \big\} \leq  z_D+R(D^+).$
Taking the maximum over all  $m\in D$ proves \eqref{dy_rec}.

At dyadic level $j$, the interval $(0,M]$ is partitioned into
$2^j$ dyadic subintervals
\begin{align*}
 D_{j,k}
 =
 \big(kM2^{-j},(k+1)M2^{-j}\big],
 \quad k=0,\ldots,2^j-1,
\end{align*}
each of length
$ \ell_j=M2^{-j}$,
  $0\le j<L$.
Define
\begin{align}\label{def_ZJ}
 Z_j :=  \max\{  z_D:  D\text{ is a dyadic interval   at level $j$} \}.
\end{align}
Iterating \eqref{dy_rec} from the root down to singleton sets gives
\begin{align}\label{cut_sum}
 R((0,M])
 \leq
 \sum_{j=0}^{L-1}Z_j.
\end{align}
Indeed, at each generation one pays at most the largest $z_D$ on that
level, while at the final level the cut maximal function of a singleton
is zero.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\bf Step 3: Estimate each dyadic scale and sum over the scales.}
Fix a level $j$.  There are
$M/\ell_j$
dyadic intervals of length $\ell_j$.  For each such interval  $D$,

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{ZD4}
 z_D^4
 =
 \min\{|S_{D^-}|,|S_{D^+}|\}^4
 \le
 S_{D^-}^2S_{D^+}^2.
\end{align}
After intersecting $D^-$ and $D^+$ with $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, the two
sets remain adjacent integer intervals.  If one of them is empty, then
$z_D=0$.  Otherwise, by \eqref{abs_adj} and \eqref{ZD4},
we have

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}[z_D^4]
 \le
 C_1N^{1-\alpha}\ell_j^{1+\alpha}.
\end{align*}
By the definition \eqref{def_ZJ} of $Z_j$,
we can write, with $M<2N$,

\noindent
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}[Z_j^4]
 \le
 \sum_{|D|=\ell_j}\mathbb{E}[z_D^4]
 \le
 \frac{M}{\ell_j}
 C_1N^{1-\alpha}\ell_j^{1+\alpha}
 =
 C_1MN^{1-\alpha}\ell_j^\alpha 
 \le
 2C_1N^{2-\alpha}\ell_j^\alpha .
 \label{Z4_bd}
\end{align}
 

\noindent
Therefore,
 $\|Z_j\|_2 \le  \|Z_j\|_4  \le C_1'  N^{\frac{1}{2}- \frac{\alpha}{4}}
 \ell_j^{\alpha/4}.$
Combining \eqref{cut_sum} with Minkowski's inequality yields,
with $M < 2N$,
\begin{align*}
 \|R((0,M])\|_2
 \le
 \sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\|Z_j\|_2
 &\le
 C_1' N^{\frac{1}{2}- \frac{\alpha}{4}}
 \sum_{j=0}^{L-1}
 (M2^{-j})^{\alpha/4}\\
 &\leq
2^{\frac{\alpha}{4}} C_1'  N^{\frac{1}{2} }
 \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}
 2^{-j\alpha/4}.
\end{align*}

\noindent
Since $\alpha>0$, we get
$ \|R((0,M])\|_2 \le C_{\alpha,C_1}\sqrt N$.\footnote{This is precisely where
the
 condition $\alpha>0$ is used; if
$\alpha=0$, the sum over the dyadic scales would be of order
$\log N$ rather than uniformly bounded.}
Finally,   from \eqref{abs_var}  and  \eqref{prefix_bd},
we get
\[
 \left\|
 \max_{1\le m\le N}|P_m|
 \right\|_2
 \le
 \|P_N\|_2+\|R((0,M])\|_2
 \le
 C_{\alpha,C_0,C_1}\sqrt N.
\]
Hence, the proof is completed.
\qedhere

title: Proposition
head: environment
name: \textsf{Uniform $L^p$ block bound

title: Proof
body_md:
First let $f$ be a polynomial of rank at least $d$ and set $U_I=\sum_{i\in
I}f_d(Z_i)e_i^{\otimes d}$.
By \eqref{shift_identity}, the sum in \eqref{lp_block_bd} equals
$\delta^d(U_I)$, and
\begin{align*}
 D^kU_I=\sum_{i\in I}f_d^{(k)}(Z_i)e_i^{\otimes(d+k)},
 \quad 0\le k\le d.
\end{align*}
Since $p/2\ge1$, Minkowski's and H\"older's inequalities yield
\begin{align*}
 \|D^kU_I\|_{L^p(\Omega;\mathfrak H^{\otimes(d+k)})}^2
 &\le\sum_{i,j\in I}|r_{ij}|^{d+k}
       \|f_d^{(k)}(Z_i)f_d^{(k)}(Z_j)\|_{\frac{p}{2}}\\
 &\le\|f_d^{(k)}\|_p^2
       \sum_{i,j\in I}|r_{ij}|^{d+k}
 \le K  |I|  \,\|f_d^{(k)}\|_p^2.
\end{align*}
Here all marginals are standard normal and $|r_{ij}|\le1$.
Combining this with \eqref{meyer_div} and \eqref{shift_sob} proves
\eqref{lp_block_bd} for polynomials, uniformly in their degree.

To pass to a general $f\in L^p(\gamma)$, choose polynomials
$a_m\to f$ in $L^p(\gamma)$; see, e.g.,
\cite[Proposition~1.1.5]{NP12}.
It is well known that the finite-rank projection $\Pi_{<d}$ is bounded on $L^p(\gamma)$.
Indeed, as a consequence of H\"older's inequality, 
we have, with $p' = p/(p-1)$,

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \|\Pi_{<d}a\|_p
 &\le \sum_{q=0}^{d-1}
 |\langle a,h_q\rangle_{L^2(\gamma)}|\,\|h_q\|_p
 \le \bigg( \sum_{q=0}^{d-1}  \|h_q\|_p\|h_q\|_{p'} \bigg) \|a\|_p.
\end{align*}



Since $\Pi_{<d}f=0$, we deduce from the above bound that 
$\Pi_{<d}a_m = \Pi_{<d}(a_m-f) \to 0$ in $L^p(\gamma)$,
and thus
the polynomials
$f_m=a_m-\Pi_{<d}a_m$
have Hermite rank at least $d$ and satisfy
$f_m\to f$ in $L^p(\gamma)$.  For every fixed finite set $I$,
$\|\sum_{i\in I}(f_m-f)(Z_i) \|_p
 \le |I|\,\|f_m-f\|_p
 \to 0.$
Passing to the limit yields the desired bound.
\qedhere

label: com_lem
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: \textsf{Dyadic decomposition of initial segments

title: Proof
body_md:
The case $m=0$ corresponds to the empty union.
For $1\le m\le N$, write its binary expansion as
$m=\sum_{\nu=1}^r2^{a_\nu}$
with $L\ge a_1>a_2>\cdots>a_r\ge0.$
Set $s_0=0$ and
$s_\nu=\sum_{\mu=1}^\nu2^{a_\mu}$ for $1\le\nu\le r$.
Since $s_r=m$, 
the intervals
 $D_\nu=\{s_{\nu-1}+1,\ldots,s_\nu\}$,
$1\le\nu\le r$,
are pairwise disjoint
 and satisfy
$
 \{1,\ldots,m\}=\bigcup_{\nu=1}^rD_\nu.
$
Moreover, $|D_\nu|=2^{a_\nu}$ and $s_{\nu-1}$ is a multiple
of $2^{a_\nu}$, because $a_\mu>a_\nu$ for every $\mu<\nu$.
Hence $D_\nu\in\mathcal D_{2^{a_\nu}}$.
The exponents are distinct, so at most one interval of each
dyadic length occurs.
See Figure~\ref{fig2} for the example $m=23$.

For each $m$, the triangle inequality therefore gives
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{k=1}^m x_k\right|
 &\le \sum_{\nu=1}^r
       \left|\sum_{k\in D_\nu}x_k\right|
       \le
 \sum_{\substack{\ell\le N\\ \ell\ {\rm dyadic}}}
 \max_{D\in\mathcal D_\ell}
 \left|\sum_{k\in D}x_k\right|.
\end{align*}
Taking the maximum over $m$ proves \eqref{use2a}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $N=2^L$ be the smallest power of two with $N\ge n$, so that
$n\le N<2n$, and define
$f(Z_k)=0$ for $n<k\le N$.
For $D\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$, write
\[
 S_D=\sum_{k\in D}f(Z_k).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{com_lem}, every initial segment
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$ is the disjoint union of at most one interval
from each dyadic partition.  Hence
\begin{align*}
 \max_{0\le m\le n}
 \left|\sum_{k=1}^m f(Z_k)\right|
 \le
 \sum_{j=0}^L
 \max_{D\in\mathcal D_{N2^{-j}}}|S_D|.
\end{align*}

For each $0\le j\le L$, the partition
$\mathcal D_{N2^{-j}}$ contains $2^j$ intervals, each of
length $N2^{-j}$. 
Then,  Proposition~\ref{lp_block}, applied to
$D\cap\{1,\ldots,n\}$, gives

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \left\|  \max_{D\in\mathcal D_{N2^{-j}}}|S_D|  \right\|_p
 \le
 \left(  \sum_{D\in\mathcal D_{N2^{-j}}}   \|S_D\|_p^p  \right)^{1/p}
 &\le
 \left[  2^j  \left( C_{p,d}\sqrt{K N2^{-j}}\,\|f\|_p  \right)^p \right]^{1/p}\\
 &= C_{p,d}\sqrt{KN}\,\|f\|_p\, 2^{-j(\frac12-\frac1p)}.
\end{align*}

\noindent
For $p>2$, the geometric series satisfies
\begin{align}\label{lp_geometric}
 \sum_{j=0}^L
 2^{-j(\frac12-\frac1p)}
 &\le
 \sum_{j=0}^\infty
 2^{-j(\frac12-\frac1p)}
 =
  \big( 1-2^{\frac1p-\frac12}  \big)^{-1}.
\end{align}

\noindent
Therefore, by Minkowski's inequality and $N<2n$,
\begin{align}\label{lp_max_proof}
 \left\|
 \max_{0\le m\le n}
 \left|\sum_{k=1}^m f(Z_k)\right|
 \right\|_p
 &\le
 C_{p,d}\sqrt{KN}\,\|f\|_p
 \sum_{j=0}^L
 2^{-j(\frac12-\frac1p)}\le
 \frac{C_{p,d}\sqrt{Kn}}
 {1-2^{\frac1p-\frac12}}\,
 \|f\|_p.
\end{align}
This proves \eqref{ns_bdd} for $p>2$.
\qedhere

label: clip_prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{clip_prop}
The functions $g_n$ have vanishing Hermite coefficients below
order $d$ and satisfy
\begin{align}\label{g_mom}
 \|g_n\|_2\le\|\varphi\|_2,
 \quad\|g_n-\varphi\|_2\longrightarrow0,
 \quad\mathbb{E}[g_n(\mathcal Z)^4]\le Cn.
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{align}\label{clip_coef}
 |\beta_{0,n}|\le n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_2^2,
 \quad
 |\beta_{q,n}|\le C_qn^{-1/2}(1+\log n)^{q/2},
\quad 1\le q<d.
\end{align}
The constants are uniform over $\|\varphi\|_2\le M$ for each
fixed $M<\infty$.
head: environment
name: \textsf{Rank-preserving truncation

label: En_prob
title: Proof
body_md:
Put  $E_n=\{|\varphi|>\sqrt n\}$ and
$ q_n=\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\mathcal Z)^2\mathbf{1}_{E_n}(\mathcal Z)].$
Then, $q_n\to0$ by dominated convergence, and
\begin{align}\label{En_prob}
 \gamma(E_n)\le \frac{q_n}{n}\le\frac{\|\varphi\|_2^2}{n}.
\end{align}
Since the Hermite coefficients of $\varphi$ below order $d$ vanish,
\begin{align}\label{beta_tail}
 \beta_{q,n}
 =-\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\mathcal Z)h_q(\mathcal Z)\mathbf{1}_{E_n}(\mathcal Z)],
 \quad 0\le q<d.
\end{align}

For $q=0$, on $E_n$ we have
$|\varphi|\le n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\varphi^2$, and thus
\begin{align}\label{beta0}
 |\beta_{0,n}|
 \le q_n n^{-\frac{1}{2}}
 \le n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_2^2.
\end{align}
For $1\le q<d$, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\begin{align}\label{beta_cs}
 |\beta_{q,n}|
 \le q_n^{\frac{1}{2}}
 \left(\int_{E_n}h_q^2\,d\gamma\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.
\end{align}
Fix $M<\infty$ with $\|\varphi\|_2\le M$.  For sufficiently
large $n$, we have $\frac{M^2}{n}\le\min\{\frac{1}{2},e^{1-q}\}$,
while 
the function $p\mapsto p(1+\log(\frac{1}{p}))^q$ is increasing on 
$(0, e^{1-q} ]$. 
Applying Lemma~\ref{rearr_lem}\textup{(i)} and
\eqref{En_prob} therefore yields
\begin{align*}
 \int_{E_n}h_q^2\,d\gamma
 \le C_q n^{-1}(1+\log n)^q.
\end{align*}
Since $q_n^{1/2}\le\|\varphi\|_2$, \eqref{beta_cs} implies
\begin{align}\label{beta_bd}
 |\beta_{q,n}|
 \le C_q n^{- 1/2}(1+\log n)^{q/2},
 \quad 1\le q<d.
\end{align}
The finitely many remaining values of $n$ are absorbed into the
constant.  When $\gamma(E_n)=0$, \eqref{beta_tail} gives
$\beta_{q,n}=0$.  The constants above can be chosen uniformly when
$\|\varphi\|_2$ ranges over a fixed bounded set.
This proves \eqref{clip_coef}.

Recall from \eqref{g_def} that
$g_n= T_n -\Pi_{<d}T_n$.  Since
$\Pi_{<d}\varphi=0$, the contraction property of the
orthogonal projection gives
\begin{align}\label{g_l2err}
 \begin{aligned}
 \|g_n\|_2
 &\le \|T_n\|_2
 \le \|\varphi\|_2,\\
 \|g_n-\varphi\|_2^2
 &\le \|T_n-\varphi\|_2^2
 =q_n\longrightarrow0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{align}

Finally, let
\begin{align}\label{def_PN}
 P_n=\Pi_{<d}T_n=\sum_{q=0}^{d-1}\beta_{q,n}h_q.
\end{align}
Since $|T_n|\le\sqrt n$,
$
 \mathbb{E}[T_n(\mathcal Z)^4]
 \le n\mathbb{E}[T_n(\mathcal Z)^2]
 \le n\|\varphi\|_2^2.
$
Moreover, from
$
 |\beta_{q,n}|
 \le \|T_n\|_2
 \le \|\varphi\|_2,
$
we can easily deduce that
\begin{align}\label{bdd_PN}
 \sup_{n\ge1}\mathbb{E}[P_n(\mathcal Z)^4]<\infty,
 \end{align}
and consequently,
 $\mathbb{E}[g_n(\mathcal Z)^4]\le Cn.$
This proves \eqref{g_mom} and thus concludes the  proof.
\qedhere

title: Lemma
head: environment

label: trunc_sq
title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{rearr_lem}\textup{(ii)}, applied to
$U=T_n(\mathcal Z)^2=\varphi(\mathcal Z)^2
\mathbf{1}_{\{|\varphi(\mathcal Z)|\le\sqrt n\}}$ with upper bound $\max\{n,2\}$, gives
\begin{align}\label{trunc_sq}
  \mathbb{E}[T_n(\mathcal Z)^2|h_q(\mathcal Z)|]
  \le C_q(1+\log n)^{\frac{q}{2}}.
\end{align}
Write $P_n=\sum_{j<d}\beta_{j,n}h_j$ as in \eqref{def_PN}.
Then,    with $g_n = T_n - P_n$, we first write
                              
                                                                       
                         

\noindent
\begin{align*}
\|B_{q,n}\|_2
&\le
\big|\mathbb{E}[T_n^2(\mathcal Z)h_q(\mathcal Z)]\big|
+\big|\mathbb{E}[P_n^2(\mathcal Z)h_q(\mathcal Z)]\big|
+2\big|\mathbb{E}[T_n(\mathcal Z)P_n(\mathcal Z)h_q(\mathcal Z)]\big|,
\end{align*}
and thus deduce \eqref{sq_low}
from
\eqref{trunc_sq}, \eqref{bdd_PN},
and
\[
 \big|\mathbb{E}[T_n(\mathcal Z)P_n(\mathcal Z)h_q(\mathcal Z)]\big|
 \leq \|T_n\|_2  \| P_n\|_4 \| h_q\|_4 \leq C_q.
\]
To prove \eqref{high_l2}, it suffices
to note that
$  \|\mathcal H_n\|_2^2
  \le \operatorname{Var}(g_n(\mathcal Z)^2)
  \le \mathbb{E}[g_n(\mathcal Z)^4]
  \le Cn,$
by orthogonality \eqref{OL_pq} and  \eqref{g_mom}.

 \medskip

Finally, we prove \eqref{sq_high} by hypercontractivity of the
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup.  For $\rho\in[0,1)$ and
$F\in L^1(\gamma)$, let
\begin{align}\label{OU_def}
 Q_\rho F(x)
 :=
 \int_{\mathbb{R}}
 F\bigl(\rho x+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,z\bigr)\,\gamma(dz).
\end{align}
For $0<\rho<1$, $Q_\rho=P_t$ in the usual
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck notation when $\rho=e^{-t}$; see, e.g.,
\cite[Definition~1.3.1]{NP12}.  In particular,
\begin{align}\label{OU_chaos}
 Q_\rho h_q=\rho^q h_q,
 \quad q\ge0.
\end{align}
Equivalently, if $(X,Y_\rho)$ is a centered Gaussian vector with
standard normal marginals and correlation $\rho$, then
\begin{align}\label{OU_corr}
 \mathbb{E}[F(X)G(Y_\rho)]
 =
 \langle F,Q_\rho G\rangle_{L^2(\gamma)}
\end{align}
for $F,G\in L^2(\gamma)$.

Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ as in the statement.  Nelson's
hypercontractivity inequality
\cite[Theorem~2.8.12]{NP12} implies that
\begin{align}\label{OU_hyper}
 Q_\varepsilon:
 L^{1+\varepsilon}(\gamma)
 \longrightarrow
 L^{\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}}(\gamma)
 \quad\text{is a contraction.}
\end{align}

Recall that
$ \theta=\frac{2\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}$,
so that
$ \frac{1}{2+2\varepsilon}
 =
 \frac{1-\theta}{2}+\frac{\theta}{4}.$
 Then, we deduce from  \eqref{g_mom} and interpolation
 that

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{interp}
 \|g_n\|_{2+2\varepsilon}^4
 &\le
 \|g_n\|_2^{4(1-\theta)}
 \|g_n\|_4^{4\theta}
 \le C n^\theta.
\end{align}

We next apply \eqref{OU_hyper} to $g_n^2$.  By H\"older's inequality,
\eqref{OU_corr}, and hypercontractivity \eqref{OU_hyper},
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}[g_n(X)^2g_n(Y_\varepsilon)^2]
 =
 \langle g_n^2,Q_\varepsilon(g_n^2)\rangle_{L^2(\gamma)}
 &\le
 \|g_n^2\|_{1+\varepsilon}
 \|Q_\varepsilon(g_n^2)\|_{\frac{1+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}}
 \notag\\
 &\le
 \|g_n^2\|_{1+\varepsilon}^2
 =
 \|g_n\|_{2+2\varepsilon}^4
 \le Cn^\theta.
 \label{hyper_sq}
\end{align}

Recall $B_{q,n}$ is the $q$th Hermite-chaos projection of
$g_n^2$.  By \eqref{OU_chaos}, \eqref{hyper_sq}, and orthogonality
relation \eqref{OL_pq},
we can write, with $v_n = \mathbb{E}[ g_n^2(\mathcal Z)]$,
\begin{align}\label{OU_series}
 \sum_{q\ge1}\varepsilon^q\|B_{q,n}\|_2^2
 &=
 \big\langle g_n^2-v_n,
 Q_\varepsilon(g_n^2-v_n)\big\rangle_{L^2(\gamma)}
 \notag\\
 &\le
 \mathbb{E}[g_n(X)^2g_n(Y_\varepsilon)^2]
 \le Cn^\theta.
\end{align}
Consequently, for $|r|\le\varepsilon$,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{q\ge d}\|B_{q,n}\|_2^2|r|^q
 &=
 \sum_{q\ge d}
 \|B_{q,n}\|_2^2\varepsilon^q
 \left(\frac{|r|}{\varepsilon}\right)^q
 \le
 \left(\frac{|r|}{\varepsilon}\right)^d
 \sum_{q\ge d}\|B_{q,n}\|_2^2\varepsilon^q
 \le
 C n^\theta |r|^d,
\end{align*}
where the factor $\varepsilon^{-d}$ is absorbed into $C$.  This proves
\eqref{sq_high} and completes the proof.
\qedhere

label: adj_prop
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: \textsf{Adjacent-block estimate

label: use1
title: Proof
body_md:
Using the Hermite-rank condition and the orthogonality relation
\eqref{OL_pq},
we obtain
\begin{align}\label{use1}
 \big|\mathbb{E}[g_n(Z_i)g_n(Z_j)]\big|
 \le \|g_n\|_2^2 |r(i,j)|^d
 \le M^2 |r(i,j)|^d.
\end{align}
Consequently, by \eqref{small_c2},
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}[S_I^2]
 =
 \sum_{i,j\in I}\mathbb{E}[g_n(Z_i)g_n(Z_j)]
  \le
 M^2\sum_{i,j\in I}|r(i,j)|^d
 \le K M^2 |I|,
\end{align*}
which proves part~\textup{(i)}.

We now prove \eqref{adj_bd}.  Put $m:=|I|+|J|$.
Expanding $\mathbb{E}[S_I^2S_J^2]$ gives a sum over
$(i,i',j,j')\in I^2\times J^2$. Since $I\cap J=\varnothing$,
there are three cases up to symmetry.

\medskip

$\bullet$ {\bf Case 1.}
Suppose $i\ne i'$ and $j\ne j'$. Since $I\cap J=\varnothing$,
the four indices $i,i',j,j'$ are all distinct. By
Lemma~\ref{diag_lem}\textup{(i)} and
$\|g_n\|_2\le\|\varphi\|_2\le M$, the total contribution of these
terms is bounded by
$
 Cm^2.
$

\medskip

$\bullet$ {\bf Case 2.}
Suppose $i=i'$ and $j\ne j'$. The case $i\ne i'$ and $j=j'$
is treated identically. By \eqref{sq_dec},
\begin{align*}
 &\mathbb{E}[g_n(Z_i)^2g_n(Z_j)g_n(Z_{j'})]\\
 &\quad=
 \|g_n\|_2^2\mathbb{E}[g_n(Z_j)g_n(Z_{j'})]
 + \bigg( \sum_{q=1}^{d-1}
   \mathbb{E}[B_{q,n}(Z_i)g_n(Z_j)g_n(Z_{j'})] \bigg)
 +\mathbb{E}[\mathcal H_n(Z_i)g_n(Z_j)g_n(Z_{j'})].
\end{align*}

For the first term, \eqref{use1} and \eqref{small_c2} give
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i\in I}
   \sum_{\substack{j,j'\in J\\ j\ne j'}}
 \|g_n\|_2^2
 \big|\mathbb{E}[g_n(Z_j)g_n(Z_{j'})]\big|
  \le C | I |
 \sum_{j\in J}\sum_{j'\in J}|r(j,j')|^d
 \le C|I||J|
 \le Cm^2.
\end{align*}

For the low-chaos terms, Lemma~\ref{diag_lem}\textup{(iii)}
together with \eqref{sq_low} yields
\[
 C\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}
 (1+\log n)^{\frac{q}{2}}m^{2-\frac{q}{2d}}.
\]
For the high-chaos term, Lemma~\ref{diag_lem}\textup{(ii)}
together with \eqref{high_l2} gives
$
 C\sqrt n\,m^{\frac{3}{2}}.
$
Thus the contribution from {\bf Case 2}
is bounded by
\begin{align}\label{one_pair}
 Cm^2
 +C\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}
 (1+\log n)^{\frac{q}{2}}m^{2-\frac{q}{2d}}
 +C\sqrt n\,m^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\end{align}

\medskip

$\bullet$ {\bf Case 3.}
Suppose $i=i'$ and $j=j'$. Since $I\cap J=\varnothing$, we have
$i\ne j$. Let
$
 v_n=\mathbb{E}[g_n(\mathcal Z)^2].
$
By orthogonality \eqref{OL_pq} and \eqref{sq_dec},
\begin{align}\label{sq_mehler}
 \mathbb{E}[g_n(Z_i)^2g_n(Z_j)^2]
 =
 v_n^2+\sum_{q\ge1}\|B_{q,n}\|_2^2 r(i,j)^q.
\end{align}
Since $v_n\le M^2$, the constant term in \eqref{sq_mehler},
summed over $I\times J$, contributes at most
$ Cm^2$.

We next treat the low-chaos terms. By \eqref{small_c2},
\begin{align}\label{pair_ld}
 \sum_{i\in I,j\in J}|r(i,j)|^d
 &\le
 K\min\{|I|,|J|\}
 \le Cm.
\end{align}
Hence, for $1\le q<d$, H\"older's inequality gives
\begin{align}
 \sum_{i\in I,j\in J}|r(i,j)|^q
 &\le
 (|I||J|)^{1-\frac{q}{d}}
 \left(
   \sum_{i\in I,j\in J}|r(i,j)|^d
 \right)^{q/d}
 \le
 Cm^{2-\frac{q}{d}}.
 \label{corr_low}
\end{align}
Combining \eqref{corr_low} with \eqref{sq_low}, the total
contribution from the orders $1\le q<d$ is bounded by
\[
 C\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}
 (1+\log n)^q m^{2-\frac{q}{d}}.
\]

For $q\ge d$, the small-correlation condition \eqref{small_c1}
gives
$ |r(i,j)|\le\varepsilon$
for $ (i,j)\in I\times J.$
Hence, for each such pair, \eqref{sq_high} yields
\[
 \sum_{q\ge d}
 \|B_{q,n}\|_2^2|r(i,j)|^q
 \le
 Cn^\theta |r(i,j)|^d,
\]
where
 $\theta=\frac{2\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}$,
and $C=C_{d,M,\varepsilon}$ is independent of $n,i,j$. Summing over
$I\times J$ and using \eqref{small_c2}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i\in I,j\in J}
 \sum_{q\ge d}
 \|B_{q,n}\|_2^2|r(i,j)|^q
 &\le
 Cn^\theta
 \sum_{i\in I,j\in J}|r(i,j)|^d
 \le
 Cn^\theta |I|
 \le
 Cn^\theta m.
\end{align*}
Therefore, the total contribution from {\bf Case 3} is bounded by
\begin{align}\label{two_pair}
 Cm^2
 +C\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}
 (1+\log n)^q m^{2-\frac{q}{d}}
 +Cn^\theta m.
\end{align}

It remains to compare the bounds above with the right-hand side of
\eqref{adj_bd}.  It suffices to take $\alpha=\frac{1}{4d}$, since the
right-hand side is nonincreasing in $\alpha$ for $m\le N$.
We have $\theta=\frac{2\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}<\frac{1}{2}$, $n\le A_0N$, and $1\le
m\le N$.
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 m^2+\sqrt n\,m^{\frac{3}{2}}+n^\theta m
 \le C N^{1-\alpha}m^{1+\alpha}.
\end{align*}
For $1\le q<d$, both $1-\alpha- \frac{q}{2d}$ and $1-\alpha- \frac{q}{d} $ are
positive,
so the remaining terms satisfy
\begin{align*}
 \frac{(1+\log n)^{\frac{q}{2}}m^{2- \frac{q}{2d} }}{N^{1-\alpha}m^{1+\alpha}}
 &\le C(1+\log N)^{\frac{q}{2}}N^{-\frac{q}{2d}}\le C,\\
 \frac{(1+\log n)^q m^{2-\frac{q}{d} }}{N^{1-\alpha}m^{1+\alpha}}
 &\le C(1+\log N)^qN^{-\frac{q}{d}}\le C.
\end{align*}
Combining {\bf Cases 1--3} proves \eqref{adj_bd}.
Hence, the proof is complete.
\qedhere

title: Lemma
head: environment
name: \textsf{Small-support estimate

label: support_split
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $u\in L^2(\gamma)$, we can expand  $|u|=\sum_{q\ge0}b_qh_q$ in $L^2(\gamma)$.
Put
$r_{ij} = \mathbb{E}[ Z_i Z_j]$.  Then, we can first deduce from 
 the orthogonality relation \eqref{OL_pq}
that

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{support_split}
 \mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{k=1}^n |u| (Z_k)\right)^2
 &\le n^2b_0^2
   +\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}b_q^2\sum_{i,j=1}^n|r_{ij}|^q
   +\sum_{q\ge d}b_q^2\sum_{i,j=1}^n|r_{ij}|^q.
\end{align}

\noindent
For the constant term,
\begin{align*}
 b_0^2=\left(\int_A |u|\,d\gamma\right)^2
 \le \gamma(A) \|u\|_2^2\le n^{-1}\|u\|_2^2.
\end{align*}
For $q\ge d$, the row bound \eqref{ns_rows} gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i,j=1}^n|r_{ij}|^q\le Kn,
\end{align*}
so the corresponding part of \eqref{support_split} is at most
$Kn\|u\|_2^2$.

If $d\ge2$ and $1\le q<d$, H\"older's inequality gives
\begin{align} \label{small_cal}
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i,j=1}^n|r_{ij}|^q
 \le K^{\frac{q}{d}}n^{2-\frac{q}{d}}
 \quad{\rm and}\quad
 b_q^2
 \le\|u\|_2^2\int_A h_q^2\,d\gamma
 &\le\|u\|_2^2\|h_q\|_{2d}^2 \gamma(A)^{1-\frac{1}{d}} \\
 &\le C_d\|u\|_2^2n^{-1+\frac{1}{d}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 b_q^2\sum_{i,j=1}^n|r_{ij}|^q
 \le C_{d,K}\|u\|_2^2n^{1+\frac{1-q}{d}}
 \le C_{d,K}n\|u\|_2^2.
\end{align*}
There are only finitely many such orders.  For $d=1$, the low-order
sum is empty.  
Therefore, combining the preceding estimates proves  \eqref{small_support_bd}.  
Finally, 
  from $\max_{m\le n}\left|\sum_{k=1}^m u(Z_k)\right|
 \le\sum_{k=1}^n|u(Z_k)|$,
 we 
prove  \eqref{bd_MA}.
\qedhere

label: herm_cut
title: Proof
body_md:
Put
$K=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}|\rho_G(k)|^d$,
and, for $M\ge d$, define
\begin{align}\label{herm_cut}
 \varphi_M=\sum_{q=d}^M c_qH_q.
\end{align}
We write $V_n^f$ and $\widehat{V_n^f}$ for \eqref{d_V} and
\eqref{hat_V}, respectively, with $f$ in place of $\varphi$.

We first prove the functional convergence for the step process
associated with the finite Hermite expansion $\varphi_M$.
For $0\le s<t\le1$, put
$I_{s,t}^{(n)}=\{\lfloor ns\rfloor+1,\ldots,\lfloor nt\rfloor\}$.
Using the orthogonality relation and $|\rho_G|\le1$, we obtain
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}\left|
 V_n^{\varphi_M}(t)-V_n^{\varphi_M}(s)
 \right|^2
&=
 \frac{1}{n}
 \sum_{i,j\in I_{s,t}^{(n)}}
 \sum_{q=d}^M q!c_q^2\rho_G(i-j)^q
 \notag\\
 &\quad\le
 \frac{\|\varphi_M\|_2^2}{n}
 \sum_{i,j\in I_{s,t}^{(n)}}
 |\rho_G(i-j)|^d
\leq
 K\|\varphi\|_2^2
 \frac{\lfloor nt\rfloor-\lfloor ns\rfloor}{n}.
 \label{disc_trunc_l2}
\end{align}
Moreover,
$V_n^{\varphi_M}(t)-V_n^{\varphi_M}(s)$
belongs to the sum of the first $M$ Wiener chaoses.
Hence, for every fixed $p>2$, hypercontractivity
\cite[Theorem~2.8.12]{NP12} and \eqref{disc_trunc_l2} yield
\begin{align}\label{disc_trunc_lp}
 \left\|
 V_n^{\varphi_M}(t)-V_n^{\varphi_M}(s)
 \right\|_p
 \le
 C_{p,M,K}\|\varphi\|_2
 \left(
 \frac{\lfloor nt\rfloor-\lfloor ns\rfloor}{n}
 \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.
\end{align}
The standard tightness criterion for partial-sum processes
(see, e.g., \cite[Lemma~3.1]{NN20}) therefore implies that
$\{V_n^{\varphi_M}\}_{n\ge1}$ is tight in $\mathbf D([0,1])$.

On the other hand, Theorem~\ref{bm_thm} gives the convergence of the
finite-dimensional distributions,
$ V_n^{\varphi_M}
 \stackrel{\rm f.d.d.}{\Longrightarrow}
 \sigma_{G,M}\mathcal{W},
$
where
$ \sigma_{G,M}^2
 =
 \sum_{q=d}^M q!c_q^2
 \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\rho_G(k)^q.
$
Thus, we have
\begin{align}\label{disc_trunc}
 V_n^{\varphi_M}
 \Longrightarrow
 \sigma_{G,M}\mathcal{W}
 \quad\text{in }\mathbf D([0,1]).
\end{align}
In particular, $\{V_n^{\varphi_M}\}_{n\ge1}$ is $C$-tight.

We now remove the Hermite truncation.  Since
$\varphi-\varphi_M$ has Hermite rank at least $d$, every finite
segment of $\mathbf G$ satisfies the assumptions of
Theorem~\ref{ns_max} with the same row-sum constant $K$.
Consequently,
\begin{align}\label{disc_approx}
 \sup_{n\ge1}
 \mathbb{E} \bigg[ \|V_n^\varphi-V_n^{\varphi_M}\|_\infty^2 \bigg]
 &=\sup_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{n}
   \mathbb{E} \bigg( \max_{0\le m\le n}
   \Big|\sum_{k=1}^m
         (\varphi-\varphi_M)(G_k)  \Big|^2 \bigg)  \notag\\
 &\le C_{d,K}\|\varphi-\varphi_M\|_2^2
 \longrightarrow0
\end{align}
as $M\to\infty$.
Moreover,
\begin{align*}
 |\sigma_G^2-\sigma_{G,M}^2|
 &\le
 \sum_{q>M}q!c_q^2
 \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}|\rho_G(k)|^q
 \le
 K\sum_{q>M}q!c_q^2
 =
 K\|\varphi-\varphi_M\|_2^2
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{align*}
Combining \eqref{disc_trunc}, \eqref{disc_approx}, and
$\sigma_{G,M}\to\sigma_G$ with Billingsley's theorem
\cite[Theorem~3.2]{Bil99}, we conclude that
$V_n^\varphi
 \Longrightarrow
 \sigma_G\mathcal{W}$
 in $\mathbf{D}([0,1])$.
Since the limit is continuous, the sequence
$\{V_n^\varphi\}_{n\ge1}$ is $C$-tight.
Finally, Proposition~1.7 of \cite{MPZ26} shows that convergence of
the step partial-sum process in $\mathbf D([0,1])$ to a continuous
limit is equivalent to convergence of its polygonal interpolation in
$\mathbf C([0,1])$.  As a result, we have
$\widehat{V_n^\varphi}  \Longrightarrow \sigma_G\mathcal{W}$
in $\mathbf{C}([0,1])$.
This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
The term
$k=0$ contributes $Ah(0)$.  For positive $k$,
by Tonelli's theorem, we have
\begin{align*}
 \int_A^{2A}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}h(ak)\,da
 &=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k}\int_{Ak}^{2Ak}h(x)\,dx\\
 &=\int_A^\infty h(x)
   \sum_{\frac{x}{2A}\le k\le \frac{x}{A}}\frac{1}{k}\,dx
 \leq (1 + \log 2)\int_A^\infty h(x)\,dx.
\end{align*}
The negative
indices are treated in the same way with \(h(-x)\).  This proves the
lemma.

label: lat_Ka
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $J_d=\int_\mathbb{R}|\rho_B(x)|^d\,dx$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lat_lem} to $h=|\rho_B|^d$ and fix $a>0$ such
that
\begin{align}\label{lat_Ka}
 K_a:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}|\rho_B(ak)|^d<\infty.
\end{align}
For $Y^{(a)}(s)=B_{as}$, stationarity gives
\begin{align*}
 &\sup_{u\in[0,1]}\sup_{i\ge0}
 \sum_{j=0}^\infty
 \big|\mathbb{E}[Y^{(a)}(1+u+i)Y^{(a)}(1+u+j)]\big|^d
 =\sup_{i\ge0}\sum_{j=0}^\infty
 |\rho_B(a(j-i))|^d\le K_a.
\end{align*}
Thus Proposition~\ref{ns_int} applies to the rescaled process.
For a function   $g\in L^2(\gamma)$ with Hermite rank at least $d$,
 put
$V_T^g(t)=T^{-\frac{1}{2}}\int_0^{Tt}g(B_x)\,dx$.
Use $F_\varepsilon^{g,Y^{(a)}}$ to denote \eqref{int_proc} for
$Y^{(a)}$.  The change of variables $x=as$ gives the exact identity
\begin{align*}
 V_T^g(t)=\sqrt a\,F_{a/T}^{g,Y^{(a)}}(t).
\end{align*}
For $T\ge a$, the parameter $a/T$ belongs to $(0,1]$.
Applying \eqref{ns_intbd} on $[0,1]$ therefore yields
\begin{align}\label{cont_max}
 \sup_{T\ge a}\mathbb{E}\Big[ \|V_T^g\|_\infty^2 \Big]
 \le C_{a,d,K_a}\|g\|_2^2.
\end{align}
In particular, with $\varphi_M$ as in \eqref{herm_cut},
\begin{align}\label{cont_approx}
 \sup_{T\ge a}\mathbb{E}\Big[   \|V_T^\varphi-V_T^{\varphi_M}\|_\infty^2 \Big]
 \le C_{a,d,K_a}\|\varphi-\varphi_M\|_2^2
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{align}

For completeness, we verify the increment bound for finite
Hermite expansions.  For $0\le s<t\le1$, the same argument as
in \eqref{disc_trunc_l2} gives

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E} \Big[  |V_T^{\varphi_M}(t)-V_T^{\varphi_M}(s)|^2 \Big]
 \le\frac{\|\varphi_M\|_2^2}{T}
       \int_{Ts}^{Tt}\int_{Ts}^{Tt}
       |\rho_B(x-y)|^d\,dx\,dy
 \le J_d\|\varphi\|_2^2(t-s).
\end{align*}
Hypercontractivity on the finitely many chaoses, followed by the
Kolmogorov tightness criterion,
implies
tightness of $(V^{\varphi_M}_T)_{T\geq a}$ in $\mathbf{C}([0,1])$.  The
finite-dimensional continuous Breuer--Major theorem recalled
in the introduction identifies the limit:
\begin{align}\label{cont_poly}
 V_T^{\varphi_M}\Longrightarrow\sigma_M\mathcal{W}
 \quad\text{in }\mathbf{C}([0,1]).
\end{align}
Here $\sigma_M^2$ is \eqref{c_var} truncated at order $M$, and
$ |\sigma_{\varphi,B}^2-\sigma_M^2|
 \le J_d\|\varphi-\varphi_M\|_2^2\longrightarrow0.$
The series in \eqref{c_var} is therefore absolutely convergent
and nonnegative, since each $\sigma_M^2$ is a limiting variance.
Billingsley's theorem \cite[Theorem~3.2]{Bil99}, applied to
\eqref{cont_approx} and \eqref{cont_poly}, completes the proof.

label: ss_env
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: \textsf{Uniform covariance envelope

label: ss_v
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $b=\beta-\frac{\alpha}{2}\ge0$ and
$v(s)=\mathbb{E}[(\Delta_1X(s))^2]$.
Under \textup{\bf(H.1)}, the increment-variance estimate of
\cite[Lemma~4.1]{CNN20} gives
\begin{align}\label{ss_v}
 \begin{aligned}
 &v(s)=2\lambda s^{2b}(1+u_1(s)),
   \quad |u_1(s)|\le Cs^{-\tau},\quad s\ge1,\\
 &\tau=1-\alpha\ \text{if }\alpha<1,
   \quad \tau=2-\alpha\ \text{if }\alpha\ge1.
 \end{aligned}
\end{align}
The covariance assumptions ensure continuity of $v$ on $[1,\infty)$.
Its positivity, proved above, and \eqref{ss_v} imply
\begin{align}\label{ss_vcomp}
 C^{-1}s^{2b}\le v(s)\le Cs^{2b},\quad s\ge1.
\end{align}
Thus \eqref{ss_vcomp} controls the normalization factors.

By symmetry, take $t=s+h$, with $s\ge1$ and $h\ge0$.
The case where $0\le h\le1$ follows  immediately 
from $|\Phi|\le1$.

Now let us consider the range $h > 1$.
Let $c>1$ be as in {\bf(H.2)}. We further split the range into two cases. 
\begin{itemize}
\item
For $h\ge1$ with $h\le(c-1)s+c$, the comparable-time estimate in
\cite[Lemma~4.2]{CNN20} reads
\begin{align}\label{ss_u}
 \begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb{E}[\Delta_1X(s)\Delta_1X(s+h)]
   =\lambda s^{2b}\big(2a_\alpha(h)+u_2(s,s+h)\big),\\
 &|u_2(s,s+h)|
   \le C\big(s^{-1}h^{\alpha-1}+s^{\alpha-2}\big).
 \end{aligned}
\end{align}
Since $|a_\alpha(h)|\le Ch^{\alpha-2}$ for $h\ge1$, division by
$\sqrt{v(s)v(s+h)}$ leads us to 

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{ss_near}
 |\Phi(s,s+h)|
 \le C\left(\frac{s}{s+h}\right)^b
   \big(h^{\alpha-2}+s^{-1}h^{\alpha-1}+s^{\alpha-2}\big)
 \le Ch^{\alpha-2}.
\end{align}
For the last inequality, we used $h\le(2c-1)s$, $b\ge0$, and $\alpha<2$.


\item  For $h\ge(c-1)s+c$, \cite[Lemma~4.3]{CNN20} gives the following
bounds:

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{ss_farraw}
 |\mathbb{E}[\Delta_1X(s)\Delta_1X(s+h)]|
 \le C
 \begin{cases}
  s^{2\beta+\nu-2}h^{-\nu},&\alpha<1,\\
  s^{2\beta-\alpha}h^{\alpha-2},&\alpha\ge1.
 \end{cases}
\end{align}
If $\alpha\ge1$, \eqref{ss_vcomp} gives $|\Phi(s,s+h)|\le Ch^{\alpha-2}$.
If $\alpha<1$, it gives instead
\begin{align}\label{ss_far}
 |\Phi(s,s+h)|
 \le C\left(\frac{s}{s+h}\right)^b
          s^{\alpha+\nu-2}h^{-\nu}.
\end{align}
Since $b\ge0$, we have
$(s/(s+h))^b\le1$.
If $\alpha+\nu-2\ge0$, the   condition
$h\ge(c-1)s+c$, with $c>1$, implies
$s\le h/(c-1)$.  Raising this inequality to the
nonnegative power $\alpha+\nu-2$ and using
\eqref{ss_far}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 |\Phi(s,s+h)|
 \le C s^{\alpha+\nu-2}h^{-\nu}
 &\le C(c-1)^{-(\alpha+\nu-2)}
        h^{\alpha+\nu-2}h^{-\nu}\\
 &\le C h^{\alpha-2},
\end{align*}
where the fixed factor involving $c$ is absorbed
into the constant.
If $\alpha+\nu-2<0$, we instead use $s\ge1$,
which gives $s^{\alpha+\nu-2}\le1$.  Thus
\eqref{ss_far} yields
$ |\Phi(s,s+h)|\le C h^{-\nu}.$
The first case corresponds to $\nu\ge2-\alpha$,
and the second to $\nu<2-\alpha$.
Hence, for $\alpha<1$, both cases give us
$
 |\Phi(s,s+h)|
 \le C h^{-\min\{2-\alpha,\nu\}}.
$
Together with the preceding bound for $\alpha\ge1$
and  \eqref{ss_near}, 
we obtain the bound   \eqref{ss_envelope} for $h\geq 1$.
\end{itemize}
Combining this with the case $h\leq 1$, we have  \eqref{ss_envelope}
for all $s,t\geq 1$.

For the lattice fiber at $u$, we can deduce from  \eqref{ss_envelope} 
that

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \sup_{i\ge0}\sum_{j\ge0}
 |\Phi(1+u+i,1+u+j)|^d
 \le C\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}(1+|k|)^{-\kappa d},
\end{align*}
uniformly in $u\in[0,1]$.  The series is finite when $\kappa d>1$.
If $\alpha<1$, both $2-\alpha$ and $\nu$ exceed one.  If $\alpha\ge1$, the
condition $\kappa d>1$ is exactly $\alpha<2- \frac{1}{d}$.
This completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{ss_law}, it is enough to consider $F_\varepsilon^\varphi$.
For $M\ge d$, let $\varphi_M=\sum_{q=d}^M c_qH_q$.
The finite-dimensional theorem in
\cite[Theorem~1.2\textup{(1)}]{CNN20} applies to $\varphi_M$.
We briefly verify tightness for these finite expansions to identify
precisely the input used in the approximation.

We first remove the initial unit interval by setting
\begin{align*}
 U_\varepsilon^M(t)=\sqrt\varepsilon
 \int_1^{\max\{1,\frac{t}{\varepsilon}\}}\varphi_M(Y(s))\,ds.
\end{align*}
Its $L^2$ uniform distance from $F_\varepsilon^{\varphi_M}$ is at most
$\sqrt\varepsilon\,\|\varphi_M\|_2$, by \eqref{cell_l2}.
For $s,t\ge1$, since the Hermite rank of $\varphi_M$ is at least $d$,
we have 

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 |\mathbb{E}[\varphi_M(Y(s))\varphi_M(Y(t))]|
 \le\|\varphi_M\|_2^2|\Phi(s,t)|^d.
\end{align*}
Since $\kappa d>1$, Lemma~\ref{ss_env} makes the right-hand side
integrable in $t$ uniformly in $s$.  Thus
$\| U_\varepsilon^M(t)-U_\varepsilon^M(s)\|^2_2\le C|t-s|$ on $[0,1]$.
Each increment belongs to the sum of Gaussian chaoses of orders
$d,\ldots,M$. 
Therefore, by  hypercontractivity
\cite[Theorem 2.8.12]{NP12}, 
we have for any fixed $p>2$:

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \|U_\varepsilon^M(t)-U_\varepsilon^M(s)\|_p
 \le C_{p,M}\sqrt{|t-s|}.
\end{align*}
The Kolmogorov tightness criterion applies since $U_\varepsilon^M(0)=0$.
Combining this with the finite-dimensional limit yields
\begin{align}\label{ss_poly}
 F_\varepsilon^{\varphi_M}\Longrightarrow\sigma_{\varphi_M,\alpha}\mathcal{W}
 \quad\text{in }\mathbf{C}([0,1]).
\end{align}

The difference $\varphi-\varphi_M$ has vanishing Hermite coefficients
below order $d$.  Then, it follows from Lemma~\ref{ss_env} and Proposition~\ref{ns_int} 
that

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{ss_approx}
 \sup_{0<\varepsilon\le1}
 \mathbb{E} \big[ \|F_\varepsilon^\varphi-F_\varepsilon^{\varphi_M}\|_\infty^2 \big]
 \le C_{X,d}\|\varphi-\varphi_M\|_2^2\longrightarrow0.
\end{align}
The constant does not depend on $M$.
Finally, $|a_\alpha|\le1$ and $a_\alpha\in L^d(\mathbb{R})$ imply
\begin{align*}
 |\sigma_{\varphi,\alpha}^2-\sigma_{\varphi_M,\alpha}^2|
 \le\|\varphi-\varphi_M\|_2^2
       \int_\mathbb{R}|a_\alpha(h)|^d\,dh\longrightarrow0.
\end{align*}

\noindent
Thus, the desired functional CLT \eqref{ss_fclt}
follows from Billingsley's theorem  (\cite[Theorem~3.2]{Bil99})
together with
\eqref{ss_poly} and \eqref{ss_approx}.
\qedhere

name: \textsf{Critical covariance comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\kappa=2-\alpha=1/d$ and $b=\beta- \frac{\alpha}{2}$.
By symmetry, it suffices to consider $0\le s\le t\le L$.
The regions where $s<1$ or $t-s<1$ contribute at most
$O(L)$.
We therefore restrict to $s\ge1$ and $h=t-s\ge1$.

Let $c_0=\min\{1,c-1\}>0$
with  $c > 1$ as in \textup{\bf(H.2)}.
First suppose that $1\le h\le c_0s$.
From  \eqref{ss_u} 
and \eqref{ss_v}, we can write
\begin{align*}
 \Phi(s,s+h)
 &=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\Delta_1X(s)\Delta_1X(s+h)]}
         {\sqrt{v(s)v(s+h)}}
         =D(s,h)\Big(a_\alpha(h)+\frac{u_2(s,s+h)}2\Big),
\end{align*}
where
\begin{align*}
 D(s,h)
 =\Big(\frac{s}{s+h}\Big)^b
  \big((1+u_1(s))(1+u_1(s+h))\big)^{-1/2}.
\end{align*}
By \eqref{ss_vcomp}, $1+u_1(t)$ is uniformly bounded
above and away from zero for $t\ge1$.
Thus $D$ is bounded.
Write $D(s,h)=A(s,h)B(s,h)$, where
\begin{align*}
 A(s,h)=(1+h/s)^{-b}
 \quad{\rm and}\quad
 B(s,h)=\big((1+u_1(s))(1+u_1(s+h))\big)^{-1/2}.
\end{align*}

\noindent
Since $0\le h/s\le1$, the mean value theorem applied
to $x\mapsto(1+x)^{-b}$ gives
$|A(s,h)-1|\le Ch/s$.
Moreover, $1+u_1(t)$ is uniformly bounded above
and away from zero by \eqref{ss_vcomp}.
Applying the mean value theorem to
$(x,y)\mapsto(xy)^{-1/2}$ therefore yields
\begin{align*}
 |B(s,h)-1|
 \le C\big(|u_1(s)|+|u_1(s+h)|\big).
\end{align*}
Using $AB-1=(A-1)B+(B-1)$, the boundedness of $B$,
and $|u_1(t)|\le Ct^{-\kappa}$ from \eqref{ss_v},
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 |D(s,h)-1|
 &\le C\Big(\frac hs+|u_1(s)|+|u_1(s+h)|\Big)
 \le C\Big(\frac hs+s^{-\kappa}\Big).
\end{align*}
Moreover, substituting $\alpha=2-\kappa$ into
\eqref{ss_u} gives
\begin{align*}
 |u_2(s,s+h)|
 &\le C\left(s^{-1}h^{1-\kappa}+s^{-\kappa}\right)
 =Ch^{-\kappa}
   \Big(\frac hs+\Big(\frac hs\Big)^\kappa\Big).
\end{align*}
Since $|a_\alpha(h)|\le Ch^{-\kappa}$ and
$h/s\le1$, we obtain, using $0<\kappa\le1$,
\begin{align}\label{kap1}
 |\Phi(s,s+h)-a_\alpha(h)|
 \le Ch^{-\kappa}
 \Big(\Big(\frac hs\Big)^\kappa+s^{-\kappa}\Big).
\end{align}
The same estimates give
\begin{align}\label{kap2}
|\Phi(s,s+h)|+|a_\alpha(h)|\le Ch^{-\kappa}.
\end{align}
Then, using  $\kappa d=1$
and
$|x^d-y^d|\le d|x-y|(|x|+|y|)^{d-1}$,
we can deduce from \eqref{kap1}--\eqref{kap2} that

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{crit_local}
 |\Phi(s,s+h)^d-a_\alpha(h)^d|
 \le Ch^{-1}
 \Big(\Big(\frac hs \Big)^\kappa+s^{-\kappa}\Big).
\end{align}

\noindent
Since $c_0\le1$, 
we have
$\min\{c_0s,L-s\} \leq s$
and thus by  enlarging  the $h$-integration range to $[1,s]$,
we can bound the contribution of this region by

\noindent 
\begin{align*}
 C\int_1^L\left(
 s^{-\kappa}\int_1^s h^{\kappa-1}\,dh
 +s^{-\kappa}\log s\right)\,ds
 \le CL.
\end{align*}



It remains to consider $s\ge1$, $h\ge1$, and
$h>c_0s$.
First note that

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 |\Phi(s,s+h)^d-a_\alpha(h)^d|
 &\le |\Phi(s,s+h)|^d+|a_\alpha(h)|^d\\
 &\le Ch^{-\kappa d}=Ch^{-1}.
\end{align*}

\noindent
For each fixed $h$, the allowed $s$-interval has
length at most $h/c_0$.  Hence this region contributes
at most $O(L)$.
Combining these estimates yields
 \eqref{crit_compare}.

Write
$J(x)=\int_0^x\int_0^x a_\alpha(t-s)^d\,ds\,dt$.
Here and below, $f(x)\sim g(x)$ means
$f(x)/g(x)\to1$ as $x\to\infty$.
For $d\ge2$, we have $\alpha=2- \frac1 d>1$.
 Taylor expansion, with cancellation of the odd-order terms, 
 allows us to obatin
 
 \noindent
\begin{align*}
 a_\alpha(h)
 &=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}2h^{\alpha-2}
   +O(h^{\alpha-4})
 \sim A_dh^{-1/d},
\end{align*}
where $A_d=\alpha(\alpha-1)/2 = \frac{(2d-1)(d-1)}{2d^2}>0$.
Consequently,
$a_\alpha(h)^d\sim A_d^d/h$ as $h\to\infty$.
As a result, we have the following asymptotic 

\noindent
\begin{align}\label{crit_stat}
 J(x)=2\int_0^x(x-h)a_\alpha(h)^d\,dh
 \sim2A_d^d x\log x.
\end{align}




For $d=1$, $\alpha=1$ and $a_1(h)=(1-|h|)_+$, so $J(x)=O(x)$.
For an even translation kernel, the rectangular integral equals
\begin{align*}
 \int_0^{Lu}\int_0^{Lv}a_\alpha(t-s)^d\,ds\,dt
 =\frac{1}{2}\big(J(Lu)+J(Lv)-J(L|u-v|)\big).
\end{align*}
Dividing by $L\log L$ and using \eqref{crit_stat} gives the limit in
\eqref{crit_covlim} for $a_\alpha$.
The absolute error on this rectangle is $O(L)$ by
\eqref{crit_compare} on the containing square.
This completes the proof.
\qedhere

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the fixed-chaos limit, with its variance given by
Lemma~\ref{ss_critcov}, and then remove the higher chaoses using
Proposition~\ref{ns_int}.  Put $L= 1/\varepsilon \ge e$ and define
\begin{align*}
 U_L(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L\log L}}
 \int_1^{\max\{1,Lt\}}H_d(Y(s))\,ds.
\end{align*}

\noindent
Note that
removing $[0,1]$ changes the path supremum in $L^2$ by at most
$\frac{\|H_d\|_2}{\sqrt{L\log L}}$, by \eqref{cell_l2}.
Now let us  represent $Y(s)=\mathcal{X}(e_s)$ with $\mathcal{X}$
isonormal over a separable Hilbert space $\mathfrak{H}$,
where
$\|e_s\|_{\mathfrak{H}}=1$ and 
$\langle e_s,e_t\rangle_{\mathfrak{H}}=\Phi(s,t)$.
Let $I_d$ denote the $d$th multiple  integral operator
such that
$\mathbb{E}[I_d(f)I_d(g)]=d!\langle f,g\rangle_{\mathfrak{H}^{\otimes d}}$
for any symmetric  $f, g\in\mathfrak{H}^{\otimes d}$, and
let  $\otimes_r$ denote
the $r$th contraction;
see \cite[Section~2]{CNN20}
and \cite{NP12} for any unexplained notation. 
Then $U_L(t)=I_d(k_{L,t})$, with\footnote{The continuity of $\Phi$ on $[1,\infty)^2$ implies
that $s\mapsto e_s\in\mathfrak H$ is continuous,
since
 $\|e_s-e_t\|_{\mathfrak H}^2
 =2\big(1-\Phi(s,t)\big) \to 0$
as $t\to s$.
We may take $\mathfrak H$ to be the closed linear
span of $\{e_s:s\ge1\}$.
By continuity, the vectors with rational indices
have the same closed linear span, so $\mathfrak H$
is separable.
Moreover, since $\|e_s\|_{\mathfrak H}=1$,
a telescoping expansion of the tensor product gives
 $\|e_s^{\otimes d}-e_t^{\otimes d}\|
 \le d\|e_s-e_t\|_{\mathfrak H}.$
Thus $s\mapsto e_s^{\otimes d}$ is continuous
and has norm one, so its integral over any compact
interval exists as a Bochner integral in
$\mathfrak H^{\odot d}$.
The map $I_d:\mathfrak H^{\odot d}\to L^2(\Omega)$
is bounded and linear, and therefore commutes
with this integral.
Together with
$I_d(e_s^{\otimes d})=H_d(Y(s))$,
this justifies $U_L(t)=I_d(k_{L,t})$.}
\begin{align*}
 k_{L,t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L\log L}}
 \int_1^{\max\{1,Lt\}}e_s^{\otimes d}\,ds.
\end{align*}



\noindent
By \eqref{OL_pq}, we have 
$ \mathbb{E}[H_d(Y(r))H_d(Y(q))]
 =d!\,\Phi(r,q)^d.$
Then,  for $s,t\in[0,1]$,
\begin{align} \label{OL_app2}
\begin{aligned} 
 \mathbb{E}[U_L(s)U_L(t)]
 &=\frac{d!}{L\log L}
   \int_1^{\max\{1,Ls\}}
   \int_1^{\max\{1,Lt\}}
   \Phi(r,q)^d\,dq\,dr\\
 &=\frac{d!}{L\log L}
   \int_0^{Ls}\int_0^{Lt}
   \Phi(r,q)^d\,dq\,dr
   +O\big((\log L)^{-1}\big)
\end{aligned}
\end{align}
as $L\to+\infty$.
                                                
                                                   
                                     
Thus, we can deduce from    \eqref{crit_covlim}
that  $ \mathbb{E}[U_L(s)U_L(t)] \to  2d!A_d^d(s\wedge t).$


 

For $d\ge2$, we verify the contraction condition for CLT on  a  fixed chaos
\cite{NP05} 
and its multivariate extension in  \cite{PT05},
in the form recalled in \cite[Theorem~2.1]{CNN20}.
Fix $r\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}$ and write $a=r/d \in(0,1)$.
In the convolution estimates below, function norms are Lebesgue norms
on $\mathbb{R}$, while tensor norms are taken in the relevant tensor powers of $\mathfrak{H}$.
Let $M=L+2$ and define the even kernels
\begin{align*}
 f_M(x)&=(1+|x|)^{-a}\mathbf{1}_{\{|x|\le M\}}
 \quad{\rm and}\quad
 g_M(x)=(1+|x|)^{-(1-a)}\mathbf{1}_{\{|x|\le M\}}.
\end{align*}
Write $\mathbf x=(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)$ and set
\begin{align*}
 J_M=\int_{[1,M]^4}\prod_{i=1}^2
 f_M(x_{2i-1}-x_{2i})g_M(x_i-x_{i+2})\,d\mathbf x.
\end{align*}
The envelope \eqref{ss_envelope} implies, uniformly for $t\in[0,1]$,
\begin{align}\label{crit_ctr}
 \|k_{L,t}\otimes_r k_{L,t}\|^2
 \le\frac{CJ_M}{L^2(\log L)^2}
 \le\frac{CM\|f_M*g_M\|_2^2}{L^2(\log L)^2}.
\end{align}
For the last inequality, fix $x_1$ and extend the other three integrals
to $\mathbb{R}$; the two convolutions give $\|f_M*g_M\|_2^2$.
Choose $p=\frac{2}{1+a}$ and $q=\frac{2}{2-a}$, so $ \frac{1}{p}+
\frac{1}{q}=\frac{3}{2}$.
Direct integration and Young's inequality yield
\begin{align*}
 \|f_M\|_p\le C M^{\frac{1-a}{2}},
 \quad\|g_M\|_q\le C M^{\frac{a}{2}},
 \quad{\rm and}\quad
 \|f_M*g_M\|_2^2\le CM.
\end{align*}
Thus the squared norm of every contraction in \eqref{crit_ctr} is
$O((\log L)^{-2})$ and tends to zero.
Hence, by the fourth moment theorems \cite[Theorem~2.1]{CNN20},
 together with the covariance limit,
 we obtain the finite-dimensional convergences. 

When $d=1$, the vector is already Gaussian and its covariance tends to
zero, so the same conclusion holds without a contraction argument.

For tightness, let $0\le s\le t\le1$.
The integration interval for $U_L(t)-U_L(s)$ has length
$\ell\le L(t-s)$.  The envelope \eqref{ss_envelope} with $\kappa d=1$
and an application of \eqref{OL_pq} as in \eqref{OL_app2}
 imply 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}\big[ |U_L(t)-U_L(s)|^2 \big]
 \le\frac{C\ell\log(e+\ell)}{L\log L}
 \le C(t-s).
\end{align*}
Then, by
hypercontractivity applied on the   $d$th chaos,
we get the corresponding
$L^p$ bound by  $C_{p,d}|t-s|^{\frac{1}{2}}$ for every $p>2$.
  Consequently, it follows from the Kolmogorov tightness criterion 
  that 
\begin{align*}
 \frac{F_{1/L}^{H_d}}{\sqrt{\log L}}
 \Longrightarrow\sqrt{2d!A_d^d}\,\mathcal{W}
 \quad\text{in }\mathbf{C}([0,1]).
\end{align*}

Finally, write $\varphi=c_dH_d+r_d$.  The remainder $r_d$ has Hermite rank at least $d+1$.  Since
$\kappa (d+1)=\frac{d+1}{d}>1$, Lemma~\ref{ss_env} supplies the fiber
row-sum bound at rank threshold $d+1$.  Proposition~\ref{ns_int} then gives
\begin{align}\label{crit_rem}
 \mathbb{E}\bigg( \left\|
 \frac{F_\varepsilon^{r_d}}{\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}}
 \right\|_\infty^2 \bigg)
 \le\frac{C_{X,d}\|r_d\|_2^2}{\log(1/\varepsilon)}
 \xrightarrow{\varepsilon\to 0}0.
\end{align}
Combining the leading-chaos limit with \eqref{crit_rem}, and then using
\eqref{ss_law}, proves the result.

The factor two in \eqref{crit_var} comes from the two symmetric
triangles in the covariance integral \eqref{crit_stat}.
The resulting constant differs from the one printed in
\cite[equation~(1.24), p.~153]{CNN20}; our normalization follows
directly from Lemma~\ref{ss_critcov} and agrees with the stationary

name: \textsf{Normalization of the critical variance

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove part~\textup{(i)}.  The case $q=0$ is immediate, so
assume $q\ge1$.  Since
$
 |h_q(x)|\le C_q(1+|x|^q),
$
it is enough to control $\int_A |x|^{2q}\,\gamma(dx)$.  Put
$p=\gamma(A)\le\frac{1}{2}$.  If $p=0$, there is nothing to prove;
hence assume $p>0$.  By Fubini and the Gaussian tail
bound,
we have

\noindent
\begin{align*}
 \int_A |x|^{2q}\,\gamma(dx)
  = \int_\mathbb{R}  \bigg( \int_0^{|x|} 2q  r^{2q-1} dr \bigg) \mathbf{1}_A(x) \gamma(dx)
&= 2q\int_0^\infty r^{2q-1}
 \gamma\big(A\cap\{|x|>r\}\big)\,dr\\
 &\le
 2q\int_0^\infty r^{2q-1}
 \min\{p,2e^{-\frac{r^2}{2}}\}\,dr.
\end{align*}
Set $R=\sqrt{2\log(\frac{2}{p})}$,
so that $2e^{-\frac{R^2}{2}}=p$.  Splitting the preceding integral at $R$
gives
\begin{align*}
 \int_A |x|^{2q}\,\gamma(dx)
 &\le
 2qp\int_0^R r^{2q-1}\,dr
 +4q\int_R^\infty r^{2q-1}e^{-\frac{r^2}{2}}\,dr\\
 &=pR^{2q}
 +2^{q+1} q   \int_{\frac{R^2}{2}}^\infty u^{q-1}e^{-u}\,du
 \quad\text{(with $u=\frac{r^2}{2}$)} \\
 &\leq pR^{2q} +   C_q e^{-\frac{R^2}{2}}(1+R^{2q-2}),
\end{align*}
where $C_q$ depends only on $q$ and may vary from line to line.
Since $2e^{-\frac{R^2}{2}}=p$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \int_A |x|^{2q}\,\gamma(dx)
 \le C_q p(1+R^{2q})
 \le C_q p\bigl(1+\log( 1/p)\bigr)^q.
\end{align*}
Together with $h_q(x)^2\le C_q(1+|x|^{2q})$, this proves
\eqref{set_rearr}.

\medskip

We next prove part~\textup{(ii)}.  Again, the case $q=0$ is
immediate.  For $q\ge1$, using
$|h_q(x)|\le C_q(1+|x|^q)$, we have
$ \mathbb{E}[U|h_q(\mathcal Z)|] \leq C_q\mathbb{E}[U]  +C_q\mathbb{E}[U|\mathcal Z|^q].$
For any $R>0$, the assumptions $0\le U\le M$ and $\mathbb{E}[U]\le C_0$
yield
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}[U|\mathcal Z|^q]
 \le
 R^q\mathbb{E}[U]
 +M\mathbb{E}\big[|\mathcal Z|^q\mathbf{1}_{\{|\mathcal Z|>R\}}\big]
 &\le
 C_0R^q
 +M\|\mathcal Z^q\|_2
   \mathbb{P}(|\mathcal Z|>R)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
 &\le
  C_0R^q+C_qM e^{-\frac{R^2}{4}}.
\end{align*}
Take
 $R=2\sqrt{\log M}$,
which is well defined for $M\ge2$.
Then,
 $M e^{-\frac{R^2}{4}}=1$
and thus,
 \eqref{wt_rearr} follows immediately.
